items.name: narration_en
items.direction: Narrate this as a dry, deadpan storyteller for a fast-paced animated history-and-science Short. PACE IS IMPORTANT: brisk and quick, about 3.7 words per second, like a fast-talking Shorts narrator; no slow drawn-out words and no long pauses (keep every pause under half a second). One steady voice and one steady energy from start to finish: warm, quietly amused, never shouting. A tiny comic beat before 'Unluckily' and before the final line only. Do not change character or tone between lines.
lines: Narrator
One drill hole drained an entire lake... in a single morning.
Narrator
November twentieth, nineteen eighty. Lake Peigneur, Louisiana.
Narrator
A calm freshwater lake. Ten feet deep. A fisherman out in his little boat.
Narrator
On the water, an oil rig was drilling for Texaco. Right underneath the lake, fifty-five miners were digging salt.
Narrator
Then the drill got stuck, twelve hundred feet down.
Narrator
Two and a half hours later, the rig started to tilt.
Narrator
The drill had punched through the roof of the mine. And the lake poured in.
Narrator
A whirlpool opened up. It swallowed the rig. A tugboat. Eleven barges. Sixty-five acres of land.
Narrator
The canal even flowed backwards, making a hundred-and-sixty-four-foot waterfall.
Narrator
Luckily, every person got out. Unluckily... the lake did not.
Narrator
Think of a bathtub. Pull the plug, and everything goes down the drain. The lake was the tub. The mine was the drain. And the drill... pulled the plug.
Narrator
Worse, fresh water dissolves salt, so the hole kept getting wider.
Narrator
The official report blamed nobody. Nobody could say if the drill was in the wrong place... or the map was.
Narrator
The settlement, three years later: thirty-two million dollars.
Narrator
Days later, nine of the eleven barges floated back up. Like nothing happened.
Narrator
The lake is still there. It's just twenty times deeper.
